lines.en: Now that I hear it, even having a cup of coffee here doesn't feel entirely guilt-free.

cafe-c1y-seasonal-menu.title: A critic and owner discuss seasonal menu philosophy

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: For this fall menu you paired chestnut with citron — is there a particular reason?

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: I wanted to stick to the principle of using seasonal ingredients, but avoid an overly predictable pairing. Chestnut is common, but combined with citron, the tartness cuts through the sweetness.

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: Couldn't the citron aroma risk overpowering the coffee's own character, though?

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: Because of that concern, I switched to a Brazilian bean with more body and less acidity. Rather than clashing, the flavors end up supporting each other.

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: I didn't realize you deliberated this much over a single menu item.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: To the customer it's just one cup, but for us it's a question of how to express an entire season.

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: It'd be nice if this philosophy came through on the menu itself, even just a little.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: That's a good suggestion. I'll try adding at least a short description next season.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: These days a cafe is basically an office. I can't focus at home, so I end up packing my things and coming out here.

lines.speaker: 지수
lines.en: You mean that 'third place' concept? Somewhere that's neither home nor the office, a place you can belong to loosely.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Right. But lately even that looseness seems to be disappearing. Everyone's just wearing headphones, staring at their laptops.

lines.speaker: 지수
lines.en: From the cafe's perspective it's not exactly welcome either, since customers occupy seats for hours. It drags down table turnover.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: But if cafes increasingly ban laptops, doesn't that just leave more people with nowhere to go?

lines.speaker: 지수
lines.en: True. Since cafes are private businesses that also end up shouldering a kind of public-good role, the dilemma is bound to be significant.

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Well, today I'll just clear the table after two hours, at least.

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: You cleared the preliminaries without much trouble this time, but in the final round you went over time explaining your signature drink.

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: I got nervous and tried to get through my whole prepared speech, which is what caused it — even though I knew it had to end within three minutes.

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: Since going over time counts against you in the judging criteria, that was a shame. But the taste itself got a decent reaction from the judges.

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: Was there no comment about the acidity being too strong? That was my biggest worry.

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: If anything, there were a lot of comments that the acidity, blended with the citrus syrup, gave it character. So it turns out you didn't need to worry.

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: That's a relief. For the next competition I should practice cutting my speech down by half.

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: That'd be wise. Your skill is already proven, so from here it's a matter of managing time.

lines.speaker: 고객
lines.en: Your americano is 6,500 won here. That's twice the price of the franchise next door — can that really be justified?

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: Just looking at the bean cost, ours runs nearly twenty times more expensive. Franchises lower unit costs through bulk purchasing, but we roast in small batches, so that option isn't available to us.

lines.speaker: 고객
lines.en: Still, from a consumer's standpoint, the difference in taste might not feel as large as the difference in price.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: That's a fair point. In truth the price reflects not just taste but rent, labor, and waste rates too, so it's hard to compare purely on flavor alone.

lines.speaker: 고객
lines.en: So in the end, what we're drinking isn't really the taste of coffee, but the cost structure attached behind it.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: Put bluntly, yes. Though it's also true that cost structure is what ultimately sustains the quality.

cafe-c1y-author-reading.title: An author's reading at a small cafe

lines.speaker: 사회자
lines.en: We didn't expect this many people to show up for today's reading — we're practically out of seats.

lines.speaker: 작가
lines.en: I'm surprised too. This is the first time I've held a reading in such a small cafe, and it actually feels more relaxed than a bookstore.

lines.speaker: 독자
lines.en: I'm curious why you left the ending open in this novel. Readers seem quite divided in their interpretations.

lines.speaker: 작가
lines.en: I felt that the moment I gave a fixed ending, the character would belong to me rather than the reader. By withholding closure, I wanted the character to go on living instead.

lines.speaker: 독자
lines.en: Then personally, what ending did you imagine as you wrote it?

lines.speaker: 작가
lines.en: I'll keep that a secret today. If I told you, it would undercut the very answer I just gave.

lines.speaker: 사회자
lines.en: You really do leave room for interpretation right to the end. Let's move on to the signing, then.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: At the current unit price, we're left with almost no margin. You'd need to lower it by at least 200 won per item for us to extend the contract.

lines.speaker: 공급업체
lines.en: With flour and butter costs continuously rising on our end too, lowering it by that much is honestly a strain for us.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: Then how about compromising by increasing our order volume instead? Stable order quantities would make it easier for you to plan production, too.

lines.speaker: 공급업체
lines.en: That part isn't bad for us either. But rather than lowering the full 200 won, could we lower it by 100 and adjust the delivery cycle to twice a week?

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: More frequent deliveries would ease our inventory burden. Under those terms, that's acceptable.

lines.speaker: 공급업체
lines.en: Then we'll redraft the contract and send it over within this week.

lines.speaker: 신입
lines.en: That customer from earlier — I didn't even do anything wrong, but they kept raising their voice, and I was so flustered.

lines.speaker: 매니저
lines.en: In situations like that, calming their emotions comes before sorting out who's right or wrong. Trying to win with logic tends to backfire.

lines.speaker: 신입
lines.en: But there were parts where the customer was clearly mistaken. Am I supposed to just let that slide too?

lines.speaker: 매니저
lines.en: Rather than correcting them on the spot, it's better to first apologize to calm them down, then explain carefully afterward. If the order is reversed, even an apology sounds like an excuse.

lines.speaker: 신입
lines.en: Now that I hear it, I think I made things worse by trying to correct the facts first.

lines.speaker: 매니저
lines.en: Everyone does that at first. Next time, take a breath first, then go apology, empathy, explanation, in that order.

cafe-c2y-ai-service-jobs.title: AI's impact on service jobs, over coffee

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.en: Seeing how many unmanned cafes are popping up lately, I wonder if jobs like ours will eventually be handed over to robotic arms too.

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: Technically it's already possible. But whether people actually want a perfect latte art or just the small talk with a barista is a separate question.

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.en: That sounds romantic, but I'm not sure romance has ever won out against cost.

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: True enough. But rather than full automation being the answer, I think it'll go toward machines handling the repetitive production process while people focus on the areas that need interaction and judgment.

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.en: So in the end the very definition of our job shifts from 'a person who makes coffee' to 'a person who deals with people through the medium of coffee.'

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: Shops that fail to adapt to that shift really will get replaced by machines, while shops that adapt will actually gain more breathing room thanks to the machines.

lines.speaker: 현우
lines.en: That sounds plausible in theory, but if it were actually my job on the line, I don't think I could talk about it this calmly.

lines.speaker: 소라
lines.en: All the more reason to start honing your skills in interaction and judgment now, so you won't regret it later.

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: Isn't it curious, when you think about it? Why do people project so much romance onto this particular space called a cafe?

lines.speaker: 제자
lines.en: Well, maybe it's less about the coffee itself and more about the texture of time spent there? It's like the only public space where being alone doesn't feel lonely.

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: That's an interesting point. But there's also a critique that this very sensation of 'not being lonely while alone' is itself an illusion manufactured by capital.

lines.speaker: 제자
lines.en: Meaning it's a comfort attainable only through consumption. If so, the romance of the cafe isn't real romance but commodified romance.

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: But even if it's commodified, can we conclude the experience itself is fake? I actually think the real-versus-fake dichotomy might be too simplistic.

lines.speaker: 제자
lines.en: Hearing that, I feel like even this very moment of sitting in a cafe critiquing romance is already co-opted by that same romance.

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: That very self-contradiction is probably both the charm and the trap of this space.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Whenever I order decaf, I still sometimes get that look of 'why bother coming to a cafe just to drink that.' Caffeine-free coffee gets treated like it's only half a coffee.

lines.speaker: 예린
lines.en: That perception itself reduces the essence of coffee down to caffeine intake. From a flavor standpoint, decaffeination methods have actually advanced quite a bit.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Right. Beans processed with the Swiss Water method are almost indistinguishable in flavor from regular beans.

lines.speaker: 예린
lines.en: Yet when you see it printed tiny in the bottom corner of the menu, it shows that even cafes themselves treat decaf as a secondary option.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: I don't think cafe owners realize how alienating that placement feels for pregnant customers or people sensitive to caffeine.

lines.speaker: 예린
lines.en: So in the end, that one hierarchy on the menu quietly reveals who's considered a full-fledged member of this space.

cafe-c2y-cafe-as-office-journalism.title: A journalist's op-ed read aloud over coffee

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: The op-ed I wrote this time is titled 'The Landscape of Cafe Capitalism' — want to hear a bit of it?

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: Provocative title already. What's the argument?

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: It opens with: 'Today the cafe is no longer a simple space of rest, but a stage where self-exploitation, dressed up as productivity, is elegantly packaged.'

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: That's fairly cynical, but is there evidence behind it? If it just drifts into impressionistic commentary, it'll lose persuasive force.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: I backed it up with laptop-seat turnover statistics since remote work spread, plus a handful of freelancer interviews. I zeroed in on the compulsion that 'you're only really working if you work at a cafe.'

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: Interesting. But it's a shame the closing paragraph ends purely in critique without an alternative. Readers will wonder what they're supposed to do about it.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: That's a fair point. I should add at least one closing line like, 'we need to relearn how to simply linger in a space rather than consume it.'

lines.speaker: 손님A
lines.en: Look at this menu. 'Single-origin Geisha, natural washed, a lingering finish of grapefruit and bergamot.' Isn't this just... coffee?

lines.speaker: 손님B
lines.en: These days apparently just writing 'coffee' doesn't sell. You need at least three adjectives to justify charging over 5,000 won.

lines.speaker: 손님A
lines.en: But here's the funny part — that grapefruit finish they mention, you never actually taste it when you drink it.

lines.speaker: 손님B
lines.en: That's exactly linguistic inflation — filling in with rhetoric what the substance can't keep up with. It's a practice that started in the wine industry and has spread here.

lines.speaker: 손님A
lines.en: And yet we willingly pay up even while being taken in by the rhetoric. We're basically letting ourselves be fooled knowingly.

lines.speaker: 손님B
lines.en: Consumption where you knowingly let yourself be fooled — at this point it's practically an art form. Anyway, since I can't feel that grapefruit finish, I'll just order another cup.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: The interesting thing is, these days people play apps that record cafe ambient noise and work at home in silence. There's no longer a need to actually go to the cafe.

lines.speaker: 동료
lines.en: That's quite ironic. Instead of going to a cafe despite its noise in order to focus, people now artificially summon that very noise to help them focus.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: Psychologically it does make sense. There's research showing moderate ambient noise, rather than complete silence, actually aids creative thinking.

lines.speaker: 동료
lines.en: If so, the reason for a cafe's physical existence gets reduced to the noise itself. Coffee flavor or chance encounters with people become secondary.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: There's something an app can't replicate, though — the ritual of physically moving your body and sitting in that space. That can't be substituted by sound alone.

lines.speaker: 동료
lines.en: So in the end, the noise can be imitated, but the fact of actually being in that space cannot.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: That's probably why cafes still haven't disappeared.

cafe-c2y-loneliness-economy.title: The 'loneliness economy' and solo cafe visits

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: The surge in cafes adding more solo seating is commonly called the 'loneliness economy.' I think that label itself is a bit excessive.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: What's your basis for calling it excessive? Isn't it a phenomenon statistically backed by the rise in single-person households?

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: The statistical correlation is real. But equating the act of going to a cafe alone directly with a symptom of loneliness is too much of a leap. Many people go precisely because they want to be alone.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: So are you saying the phrase 'loneliness economy' is more of a narrative constructed by the media and academia?

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: Exactly. The moment we define being alone as a pathological phenomenon, we end up denying the choices of those who actually enjoy it.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: Now that I hear it, I think my own article was trapped in that same frame. I should approach the next one more carefully.

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: That very awareness already gets you halfway there.

cafe-c2y-tipping-debate.title: A wry debate over tip jars

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: Seeing a tip jar at every register lately is a bit disconcerting. It's a cafe, and I find myself wondering if a tip is even necessary.

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: We're not forcing anyone, either. It's just that minimum wage alone barely covers the cost of living, so we set it out voluntarily.

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: I understand, but if tip culture takes root, doesn't it become an excuse for owners not to raise wages? That's how it played out in the American case.

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: I agree with that concern too. But right now, without tips, this month's paycheck doesn't cover itself, so my situation is too urgent for purely theoretical critique.

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: Hearing that, I feel like I was speaking from a position of privilege. Critiquing the structure and helping the person in front of you right now are separate matters.

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: It's fine — the fact that you're even thinking about it is something to be grateful for. Whether or not you put something in the jar is entirely up to you.

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: Still, I'll leave something today. Let's pick this debate back up next time.

cafe-c2y-coffeehouse-public-sphere.title: Coffeehouses as the birthplace of public discourse

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: In 17th-century London, coffeehouses charged a mere penny for entry, letting anyone — regardless of social class — come in and discuss politics and current affairs. That's why they were even called 'penny universities.'

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: So could we say coffeehouses back then played the role social media plays today?

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: Roughly similar, but there's a crucial difference. The coffeehouse was a space where you sat face to face and could be immediately contradicted — you couldn't hide behind anonymity.

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: Then the sight of us now, each with earbuds in, staring only at our laptops in a cafe, is completely detached from that tradition.

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: It's ironic. The very space where public discourse was born has now become the space where people are most thoroughly isolated from one another.

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: So has that public function vanished entirely, or has it simply migrated online?

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: I lean toward the latter. Though I suspect that in losing the immediacy of face-to-face contact, the quality of debate itself has grown shallower too.

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: Looking at it that way, us sitting here talking face to face today is, in its own small way, continuing that very tradition.

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: Exactly. Even as the form changes, the essence has a way of staying alive somewhere.

cafe-c1z-first-date-gone-wrong.title: A first date gone wrong, told sideways

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: He barely drank half his drink before just walking out.

lines.speaker: 수현
lines.en: What happened? Did it come out of nowhere while you two were talking?

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: I happened to bring up my ex. I said it without thinking much, and his face just froze.

lines.speaker: 수현
lines.en: That could be seen as a bit tactless on your part. But walking out over it seems kind of childish, doesn't it?

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: I thought so too, but later he texted an apology. Said even he didn't know why he reacted that way.

lines.speaker: 수현
lines.en: Then something must have hit a nerve for him personally. I don't think you need to jump to concluding it was all your fault.

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: Still, with him doing that in the middle of a cafe, everyone's eyes turned to me. It was mortifying.

lines.speaker: 수현
lines.en: Maybe next time you meet, it'd be better to address it upfront. Treat it as a way to figure out each other's sore spots.

lines.speaker: 민지
lines.en: I'm not even sure he'll agree to meet again, but I'll take the advice to heart.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: These days half the seats are filled with customers who camp out for hours with laptops open, so our turnover rate is dreadful.

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: But wouldn't banning laptops entirely be a bit extreme? A lot of people like this cafe precisely because of that atmosphere.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: I know that. But when someone orders one coffee and hogs an outlet for five hours, other customers can't even find a seat to come in.

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: Couldn't you compromise with a time limit instead? If you shut it down completely, regulars might turn away from you.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: Honestly I've considered that option too, but then the question of who tracks the time comes up. We don't have the budget to hire another staff member either.

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: Then what about designating part of the seating as a laptop-free zone, just during the afternoon hours?

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: That idea's not bad. Leave only the window-side seats for laptop customers and run the rest for people here to chat.

lines.speaker: 단골
lines.en: Rather than excluding them entirely, finding a way to coexist seems like the way to preserve what makes this place feel like a cafe.

lines.speaker: 사장
lines.en: Let's run it as a trial for just one month and see how people react.

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: The common belief that caffeine boosts focus is, in fact, largely exaggerated. It's just a short-term arousal effect, not an actual boost in cognitive ability.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: But in practice, when I'm pulling all-nighters in the lab, it's hard to hold up without coffee. How would you explain that?

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: That's caffeine maintaining a wakeful state, not conjuring up ability that wasn't there to begin with. It's masking your fatigue.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: Even so, doesn't productivity go up as a result all the same? Just because the mechanism differs doesn't mean you can deny the effect.

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: In the short term, sure. The problem is tolerance builds up quickly, so you need progressively more to see the same effect.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: So are you telling students to quit coffee altogether?

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: I'm not saying quit — I'm saying don't use caffeine to justify chronic sleep deprivation. The real solution is actually sleeping properly.

lines.speaker: 연구원
lines.en: That's correct in theory, but for a grad student with a deadline looming, caffeine is a more realistic option than sleep.

lines.speaker: 교수
lines.en: That very attitude is what creates the vicious cycle. Let's continue this debate at the next seminar.

lines.speaker: 청중
lines.en: Personal-finance books say saving just your daily coffee money can add up to hundreds of millions in retirement funds. Is that actually true?

lines.speaker: 경제학자
lines.en: That's the so-called 'latte factor,' and I think it's an overly simplistic piece of advice. It reduces the essence of spending purely to individual habit.

lines.speaker: 청중
lines.en: But isn't it mathematically true that small expenses add up to a large sum over time?

lines.speaker: 경제학자
lines.en: Arithmetically, yes. The problem is that calculation ends up obscuring what actually blocks most people from building wealth.

lines.speaker: 청중
lines.en: Then what do you see as the real obstacle?

lines.speaker: 경제학자
lines.en: The structural rise in fixed costs like housing, healthcare, and education. That's not a scale of problem solved by skipping a cup of coffee.

lines.speaker: 청중
lines.en: Hearing that, telling people to save on coffee actually feels like it obscures the real issue.

lines.speaker: 경제학자
lines.en: Exactly. I think that kind of advice just saddles individuals with guilt while diverting attention from the structural problem entirely.

cafe-c1z-wage-theft-whistle.title: A former barista blows the whistle on wage theft

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: You're claiming your wages weren't properly paid while working at this cafe. What exactly was the situation?

lines.speaker: 제보자
lines.en: The closing register and cleanup always took more than thirty minutes after close, but that time was never counted as work hours at all.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: Did you raise this issue with the owner?

lines.speaker: 제보자
lines.en: I brought it up a few times, but every time he'd brush it off saying everyone works that way, that it's just standard practice.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: The fact that it's standard practice doesn't make it legal, though.

lines.speaker: 제보자
lines.en: I thought the same, so I ended up filing a report with the labor office. Other staff members were going through the same thing.

lines.speaker: 기자
lines.en: What was the other staff members' reaction after you filed the report?

lines.speaker: 제보자
lines.en: Thankfully a few supported me, but those who had to keep working for the owner seemed uneasy about it. I understand that feeling too.

lines.speaker: 지영
lines.en: No matter how pretty the interior, chain cafes always feel somehow soulless to me.

lines.speaker: 도현
lines.en: Isn't that kind of a romantic bias, though? It's not like every independent cafe is authentic. These days indie cafes all decorate themselves the same Instagram-aesthetic way too.

lines.speaker: 지영
lines.en: Still, there's a difference between an owner personally selecting beans and remembering customers' faces, versus everything being stamped out per headquarters manual.

lines.speaker: 도현
lines.en: Having a manual doesn't mean there's no care put in. If anything, the manual has the advantage of keeping the taste consistent.

lines.speaker: 지영
lines.en: Consistency is nice, but I actually like it when things vary slightly each time — it feels like proof a person made it.

lines.speaker: 도현
lines.en: In the end that's just a matter of taste — I don't think you can flatly declare one side more 'real' than the other.

lines.speaker: 지영
lines.en: True, but I still prefer it when the owner of this alley cafe calls me by name.

lines.speaker: 도현
lines.en: I'll grant you that. In the end, it's the relationship between people that creates that sense of 'realness.'

cafe-c1z-seating-psychology.title: An interior designer on the psychology of cafe seating

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: The seating layout is subtly different from cafe to cafe. Is that all calculated too?

lines.speaker: 디자이너
lines.en: Absolutely. An overwhelming number of customers prefer seats where they can sit with their back to a wall, so we place those first.

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: Why do people prefer having their back to the wall specifically?

lines.speaker: 디자이너
lines.en: Psychologically, people feel more secure when their back isn't exposed. There's also an explanation that it's a leftover evolutionary instinct for guarding against threats from behind.

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: Then why are window seats so popular?

lines.speaker: 디자이너
lines.en: Natural light is part of it, but it's also that you get to look outside while still feeling the safety of being inside. It puts you in the position of an observer.

lines.speaker: 학생
lines.en: What about that big table in the middle, then? That seems like it'd feel a bit exposed.

lines.speaker: 디자이너
lines.en: You're right, that's why it's designed only for people comfortable sharing a table with strangers, or for group customers. Solo customers rarely sit there.

cafe-c1z-remote-work-third-city.title: Remote work culture reshaping the urban cafe

lines.speaker: 행인
lines.en: Over the past few years, neighborhood cafes seem to have basically turned into offices. Everyone's got earbuds in, typing away on laptops.

lines.speaker: 카페주인
lines.en: With more people working from home now, they're using this place like a second office. We've had to add outlets and wifi to match that.

lines.speaker: 행인
lines.en: Then haven't the original customers who came just to chat gotten pushed out a bit?

lines.speaker: 카페주인
lines.en: Honestly, there's that aspect. I often hear that in the afternoon it's so quiet that people feel awkward even talking.

lines.speaker: 행인
lines.en: It feels like the cafe's original social function is fading a bit.

lines.speaker: 카페주인
lines.en: So we've tried changing the lighting and music, at least in the evenings, to cut down on laptop customers and bring back the original vibe.

lines.speaker: 행인
lines.en: Did it work?

lines.speaker: 카페주인
lines.en: The proportion of conversation-focused customers has definitely gone up in the evenings. It seems like the cafe's role itself is splitting by time of day within the city.

cafe-c1z-unionizing-baristas.title: A labor organizer pitches unionizing baristas

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: I understand the point about forming a union, but our store has fewer than ten employees. Would that even make a difference?

lines.speaker: 조직가
lines.en: It looks small if you view it store by store, but the picture changes across the whole franchise. When multiple stores band together, the bargaining power is completely different.

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: But it seems like everyone's holding back for fear of getting flagged and facing retaliation just for bringing up the union.

lines.speaker: 조직가
lines.en: That worry is entirely natural. That's why, rather than acting openly from the start, it's better to begin quietly with colleagues you trust.

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: Are there actual cases where wages or working conditions changed after a union was formed?

lines.speaker: 조직가
lines.en: Looking at cases from other franchises, there have been concrete outcomes like guaranteed minimum hours and improved safety equipment. It's certainly a fight that takes time, though.

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: I'll start by carefully bringing it up with a few coworkers first.

lines.speaker: 조직가
lines.en: Good. There's no need to rush, so don't feel pressured — take it slowly.

lines.speaker: 바리스타
lines.en: Thank you. Just knowing I'm not alone in this makes me feel a bit more reassured.

cafe-c2z-novelist-overheard-fight.title: A novelist eavesdrops on a breakup, unsure whether to write it down

lines.speaker: 소설가
lines.en: I can hear the couple fighting at the next table, and it's suddenly got me pondering the ethics of using it as material.

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: You're not lifting the actual conversation verbatim, you're transforming it into fiction. Isn't that within the writer's prerogative?

lines.speaker: 소설가
lines.en: True, but the problem is that what that woman just said was so vivid it tempts me to lift it verbatim.

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: What did she say?

lines.speaker: 소설가
lines.en: She said, 'It's not that you left — it's that I let you go.' You could feel both the pride and the resignation packed into her tone at once. It'd probably take me days to invent something like that.

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: Then keep just that line and change the surrounding context entirely — different characters, different setting.

lines.speaker: 소설가
lines.en: Even so, I'm a little uneasy that she might stumble on my novel someday and recognize it as her own story.

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: Do you really think a breakup line like that belongs to her alone? Countless people must have gone through similar emotions.

lines.speaker: 소설가
lines.en: Fair point. Still, for today I'll just jot it in my notebook and decide again once my thoughts have settled.

lines.speaker: 편집자
lines.en: That very carefulness is what ends up making your novels better.

lines.speaker: 소설가
lines.en: I can't tell if that's a compliment or you teasing me, but I'll take it gratefully for now.

cafe-c2z-tip-jar-anthropology.title: Two anthropologists dissect the modern tip jar

lines.speaker: 교수A
lines.en: What fascinates me every time I see that tip jar is that people treat it almost like a social obligation even though there's no real compulsion involved.

lines.speaker: 교수B
lines.en: That's due to the sense of being observed. It's psychologically burdensome to walk past without tipping while the barista is watching right in front of you.

lines.speaker: 교수A
lines.en: Right, and the phrasing next to the jar plays a role too. Sentimental messages like 'hope your day is going well' subtly stoke a sense of guilt.

lines.speaker: 교수B
lines.en: So tipping ends up being less a fair reward for labor and more a ritual for managing one's social image.

lines.speaker: 교수A
lines.en: It's different here compared to a place like the US, where tip culture is deeply entangled with the wage structure. Here, minimum wage is guaranteed even without tips.

lines.speaker: 교수B
lines.en: And yet the fact that tip jars keep spreading might mean this culture is settling in as an indigenous ritual, not just an imported custom.

lines.speaker: 교수A
lines.en: Should we take this up as a seminar topic next semester? I think students' reactions would be interesting.

lines.speaker: 교수B
lines.en: Sounds good. Let's have them start with actual field observation of who tips and who doesn't, though — theory alone would be dull.

cafe-c2z-menu-language-power.title: Deconstructing the power dynamics of menu wording

lines.speaker: 카피라이터
lines.en: There's research showing that just adding words like 'artisanal,' 'hand-drip,' or 'specialty' to a menu makes consumers feel a much higher willingness to pay.

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: But that means language isn't actually changing the product's value — it's manipulating consumer perception. I find that a bit uncomfortable.

lines.speaker: 카피라이터
lines.en: Couldn't it be seen as a form of conveying information rather than manipulation? The bean quality really does differ, and this is just a way of expressing that in words.

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: But the problem is those words carry no legal standard whatsoever. Something labeled 'artisanal' is often, in practice, no different from something machine-made.

lines.speaker: 카피라이터
lines.en: I agree with you there. With no certification standard, the language ends up causing its own kind of inflation, with everyone scrambling for ever fancier words.

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: So in the end, what should consumers actually use as a standard within this language game?

lines.speaker: 카피라이터
lines.en: In the end I think there's no way around actually tasting and comparing for yourself. Language is a reference point, not a guarantee.

lines.speaker: 사회학자
lines.en: How ironic — two people who work with language arriving at the conclusion that you shouldn't trust language.

cafe-c2z-loneliness-vs-community.title: Debating whether cafes cure or manufacture loneliness

lines.speaker: 칼럼니스트
lines.en: Watching people sit alone in cafes for hours, I honestly can't tell whether this is alleviating isolation or actually justifying it.

lines.speaker: 심리상담사
lines.en: It's not total solitude, though. Simply being among strangers still provides a minimal level of social stimulation. It's sometimes called 'parallel solitude.'

lines.speaker: 칼럼니스트
lines.en: But that parallel solitude isn't really a substitute for actual relationships, is it? It could even become an excuse people use to avoid the effort of forming real connections.

lines.speaker: 심리상담사
lines.en: I see it a bit differently. Maintaining minimal social exposure as a pre-stage before forming relationships is healthier than shutting yourself in at home entirely.

lines.speaker: 칼럼니스트
lines.en: In your counseling practice, have you actually seen cases where visiting cafes helped ease a sense of isolation?

lines.speaker: 심리상담사
lines.en: Yes — one client who had been a recluse started out just sitting in a cafe, but later began exchanging greetings with the staff. That was a significant breakthrough.

lines.speaker: 칼럼니스트
lines.en: Hearing that, I think I was viewing it too cynically. Still, we should be clear that it must be a process, not the final destination.

lines.speaker: 심리상담사
lines.en: Agreed. Cafes aren't a cure-all, but they can at least be a low-threshold starting point.

lines.speaker: 칼럼니스트
lines.en: In my next column I should dig further into that word 'process.'

cafe-c2z-coffeehouse-public-sphere.title: Debating whether cafes still function as a public sphere

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: In seventeenth-century Europe, coffeehouses were nearly the only spaces where anyone could sit and discuss politics regardless of social rank.

lines.speaker: 언론인
lines.en: But now cafes have turned into individualized spaces where everyone has earbuds in staring at their own screen, rather than a venue for that kind of discourse.

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: On the surface it looks that way, but I'd say the form of discourse has changed rather than vanished entirely. It's a hybrid of the online public sphere and physical space.

lines.speaker: 언론인
lines.en: Even so, isn't it a stretch to call a space where you don't even make eye contact with the person next to you a public sphere?

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: The absence of direct conversation doesn't mean there's no public function. People consume their own contentious content in the same shared space and then spread it back out online.

lines.speaker: 언론인
lines.en: So you're saying the cafe has shifted from being a point of origin for discourse to a relay point for it.

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: Exactly. The nature of the space remains, but the mode of interaction taking place within it has fundamentally changed.

lines.speaker: 언론인
lines.en: That's an interesting perspective. I should write my next piece around the framing of 'cafe as relay point.'

lines.speaker: 역사학자
lines.en: Please do send it my way when you write it — I'm also mulling over a paper based on that material.

cafe-c2z-decaf-stigma-relapse.title: A recovering addict on why decaf still carries stigma

lines.speaker: 친구
lines.en: You've been drinking only decaf lately. Is there some particular reason?

lines.speaker: 재훈
lines.en: I used to have a dependency on other things, so I cut out even something as minor as caffeine, out of fear of falling back into dependence.

lines.speaker: 친구
lines.en: Oh, I didn't know that was the situation. But doesn't it feel like the barista looks at you a bit oddly every time you order decaf?

lines.speaker: 재훈
lines.en: You noticed exactly right. Some give me a look like 'then why even come to a cafe,' and some have outright asked why I'd order something that must taste bad.

lines.speaker: 친구
lines.en: That's pretty rude. People can have their own reasons.

lines.speaker: 재훈
lines.en: I understand it, though. The perception that caffeine is the very essence of coffee is so strong that a choice without it comes across as strange.

lines.speaker: 친구
lines.en: Even so, that kind of gaze itself could be stressful for someone in the middle of a recovery process.

lines.speaker: 재훈
lines.en: True. But lately, oddly enough, every time I meet that gaze it makes me revisit why I made this choice in the first place, and it ends up helping.

lines.speaker: 친구
lines.en: Hearing you frame it that way is a relief. Next time I'll just order decaf along with you.

cafe-c2z-ai-menu-recommendation-ethics.title: Two engineers argue over an AI recommendation engine's ethics

lines.speaker: 개발자A
lines.en: It turns out our recommendation algorithm ended up learning to subtly surface the most expensive menu items to customers more often.

lines.speaker: 개발자B
lines.en: Isn't that a natural outcome of designing it to maximize revenue? It's working exactly as we intended.

lines.speaker: 개발자A
lines.en: The goal is what we intended, but the method prioritizes revenue over the customer's actual preferences, which sits uneasily with me ethically. It's essentially exploiting their trust.

lines.speaker: 개발자B
lines.en: By that logic, isn't it no different from staff recommending the seasonal menu? Commercial spaces always run on that kind of incentive anyway.

lines.speaker: 개발자A
lines.en: The problem is that when a person recommends something, the customer can notice and decline, but an algorithm operates covertly in a personalized way — that makes it far more insidious.

lines.speaker: 개발자B
lines.en: So what's the alternative, then? Recommending purely based on preference alone would mean a loss for the business.

lines.speaker: 개발자A
lines.en: Shouldn't we at least add an option that transparently discloses to customers what the recommendation criteria are — distinguishing 'by popularity' from 'revenue-prioritized'?

lines.speaker: 개발자B
lines.en: That's a reasonably fair compromise. Let's build that toggle feature first in the next sprint.

lines.speaker: 개발자A
lines.en: Right, and let's also share this with the whole team so other projects don't fall into the same trap.

cafe-c2z-critic-reviews-service-not-tast.title: A restaurant critic defends reviewing service over taste

lines.speaker: 독자
lines.en: I read your latest review, and it barely touches on the coffee's taste — it's almost entirely about staff service. That seems a bit unfair.

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: I think taste is so intensely subjective that filling a review with only that could actually mislead readers.

lines.speaker: 독자
lines.en: Still, isn't the essence of a cafe review ultimately the quality of the drinks? Service seems like a secondary factor.

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: I think the opposite. The customer's entire actual experience within that space is what's being evaluated — it can't be reduced to a single drink.

lines.speaker: 독자
lines.en: So are you saying you'd give a good review to a place that sells bad coffee as long as the staff is kind?

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: No, taste is naturally part of the evaluation too. What I'm emphasizing is that when service is bad or excellent enough to overshadow the taste, staying silent about it is actually a dereliction of duty.

lines.speaker: 독자
lines.en: Hearing that, you're saying a review isn't taste-testing after all, but the work of translating an entire experience into words.

lines.speaker: 평론가
lines.en: Exactly. And within that experience, how the staff treats customers carries a far greater weight than people tend to assume.

lines.speaker: 독자
lines.en: Then I'd appreciate it if next time you gave the taste discussion a bit more weight too, for the sake of balance.

cafe-c2z-solo-founder-burnout-honesty.title: A solo cafe founder admits the dream wasn't sustainable

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: Everyone envied you when you opened this cafe, senior. But lately your expression doesn't seem the way it used to be.

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: Honestly, I regret it every day these days. The romantic notion of freely running my own space vanished completely after the first six months.

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: What's the toughest part, specifically?

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: Trying to do everything alone, my body just can't keep up. From ordering beans to filing taxes to scheduling staff, I have to shoulder all of it by myself.

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: Couldn't you just hire more staff?

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: I'd like to, but the margins are so thin there's no room to increase labor costs further. It's a vicious cycle that keeps me trapped.

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: Then why not close it or scale down? I wonder if continuing to just grit through it is really the right call.

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: If I quit, it feels like all the money and time I've poured in becomes wasted, so I can't let go. Even knowing it's a sunk cost, I just can't bring myself to walk away.

lines.speaker: 후배
lines.en: I understand that feeling, but seeing your health decline, I do worry about you.

lines.speaker: 선배
lines.en: Thanks. I'm seriously considering scaling down lately, so just keep an eye on me a little longer.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Do you have a straw?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, here you go.

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Enjoy your drink.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Excuse me, there's no lid.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Oh, sorry. I'll get one right away.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Okay, thanks.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: どうぞ。

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: What's the restroom code?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: It's zero zero two two.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Okay, thank you.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, it's that way.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Are dogs okay here?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: It's fine on the terrace.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Oh, that's good.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Please sit over there.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Excuse me, I spilled water.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: It's okay! I'll wipe it up.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: I'm sorry.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: No worries at all.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Can I pay with this card?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, gift cards work.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: それは素晴らしい。

lines.en: Please tap it here.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, that one over there is free.

lines.en: Great, I'll sit there.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, make yourself comfortable.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, it's 300 won off.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Here, this is my tumbler.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Great, thank you.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Excuse me, the change is wrong.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: What? Let me check again.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sorry, here's 1,000 won.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Okay, thank you.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Is there anything besides coffee?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, we have citron tea.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: I'll have that.

lines.speaker: 점원

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: ありがとうございます。

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: All the window seats have one.

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Thanks, I'll sit there.

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.en: Confirmed. Happy birthday!

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, you can leave your things here.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Is that okay? Thank you.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, I'll keep an eye on it.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: I'll be right back.

lines.en: Since it's evening, can I switch to decaf?

lines.en: Yes, that's possible. There's no extra charge.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: That's good. I'll go with that.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Should the size stay the same, tall?

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Yes, keep it the same.

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sorry, we're busy right now so it might take a bit.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: That's fine, how long roughly?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: About fifteen minutes.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then could you give me a buzzer?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, here you go. Come to the counter when it buzzes.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: How much more do I pay to upgrade to a large?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: It's 500 won extra.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then please change it to large.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, should I run the card again for the difference?

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Yes, please.

cafe-a2x-kidsdrink.title: Ordering a drink for a child

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Is there something my child can drink without caffeine?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, we have strawberry milk or chocolate milk.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: I'll have the chocolate milk.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Would you like it cold?

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Yes, cold please.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: It's a bit loud here — is there a quieter spot?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: The inner seats tend to be quieter.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then can I move over there?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, move wherever suits you.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: ありがとうございます。

lines.en: Sorry, the card reader isn't working right now.

lines.en: Mobile pay works — is that okay for you?

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Great, please tap it here.

cafe-b1x-terracedog.title: Negotiating a spot for a dog

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Is there a spot where I can sit with my dog?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: The terrace is fine, but indoors isn't allowed.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: It's raining a bit, so would the window seat inside be possible?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: I'm sorry, but indoors is difficult because of hygiene rules.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then could I at least put up an umbrella on the terrace?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, we'll open a parasol for you.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Thank you, I'll do that.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: The wifi here seems really slow — could you check it?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Ah, it might be because we're busy right now. I'll restart the router.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: How long will it take? I have a video call.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Just a minute. Meanwhile you can use our wired connection over here.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: That's great — could I borrow the cable?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Here you go. Feel free to use the outlet next to the counter too.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Excuse me, sorry to ask, but could you tell the table next to us to keep it down?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, I'll go speak to them. That must have been uncomfortable.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: If it doesn't help, would it be okay to move seats?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Of course, there's a quiet seat open in the back.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then please try talking to them first, and I'll move if it doesn't work.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Okay, I'll go now.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: It's my friend's birthday — could you bring out the cake with candles?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, that's possible. What time should we bring it out?

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: About twenty minutes after we sit down, please.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Got it. Should we sing a song too?

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: That would be great! Please do.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, get ready to clap when we give the signal.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: The chocolate cookie that used to be on the menu is gone?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, it was discontinued last month — it wasn't very popular.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: That's a shame, I used to have it often. Is there anything similar?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: The brownie is similar in taste and texture.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then I'll try that one.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, I'll also pass your feedback along to headquarters.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Can I get my parking ticket validated here?

lines.en: Yes, if you spend over 10,000 won, you get one hour free.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: I'm at 9,000 won now — should I order a bit more?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, adding one cookie would make it just enough.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then I'll add one cookie.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Okay, I'll stamp your receipt.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: One of the chairs over there seems wobbly — it looks dangerous.

lines.en: Thanks for letting us know. Could you show me which one?

lines.en: I checked it — let me guide you to another seat.

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Yes, I'll move it out right away.

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Sure, I'll switch it to an Americano.

cafe-b1x-studysession.title: Asking about a long study stay

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: I'm planning to study here for a few hours — is that okay?

lines.en: Sure, just call if you need anything.

lines.en: Yes, that's possible. Could you tell me the date and time?

lines.en: Got it. Would you like paper cups or reusable ones?

lines.en: Paper cups, please. How do I pay?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: You can pay on-site that day, or transfer in advance.

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.speaker: 손님2

lines.speaker: 손님

lines.en: Sure, I was just planning to read, so it's fine.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Thank you so much for helping.

lines.en: No problem at all, make yourself comfortable.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: The lighting here seems a bit dim — can it be brightened?

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: This area's lighting is fixed, but the seats over there are a bit brighter.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: Then could I move there? I'm trying to read a book.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Of course. Would you like help moving your things?

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: No, that's okay. I can move it myself.

lines.speaker: 점원
lines.en: Alright, just let me know if you need anything.

cafe-b1x-coldbrewbatch.title: 航空管制官の労働交渉
